title: Leveraging AI-Powered Writing Assistants to Enhance L2 Writing Proficiency: A Mixed-Methods Study
venue: AI and Tech in Behavioral and Social Sciences
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an AI-powered writing assistant, Grammarly, can improve L2 English writing proficiency and learner engagement compared with traditional teacher and peer feedback. The study addresses problems common in L2 writing instruction, including delayed feedback, inconsistent quality, and limited scalability, and also explores learners’ perceptions of AI feedback, including motivation, self-efficacy, and trust.

The intervention lasted 12 weeks. Sixty CEFR B2–C1 English as a foreign language learners at Ilam University in Iran were divided into an experimental group (n=30) and a control group (n=30). The experimental group used Grammarly Premium while drafting and revising eight argumentative essays, and the control group received traditional teacher and peer feedback. Quantitative data came from pre/post writing assessments scored with an IELTS-based rubric and from Coh-Metrix text analysis. For the experimental group, Grammarly usage analytics captured revisions and time-on-task. Qualitative data came from semi-structured interviews with 15 experimental-group participants.

The paper reports that the Grammarly group improved substantially more than the control group on grammar accuracy, coherence, and syntactic complexity, with large within-group effect sizes for the experimental group (reported d values from 1.40 to 1.75). The study also reports that revision frequency and time-on-task predicted writing gains, and interview data suggested increased motivation, self-efficacy, and trust in AI feedback, though students still wanted human guidance for higher-order concerns such as argumentation and organization.

For the specific verification issue raised here, this is not the alleged 2026 high-school ChatGPT motivation RCT with 25+25 students. It is a 2025 university Grammarly study with 30+30 undergraduates. The paper is internally inconsistent about design: the Methods section labels it quasi-experimental, but the participant description claims random assignment using stratified randomization and baseline equivalence testing. No motivation scale statistics are reported; motivation appears only in qualitative interview themes, so there are no extractable original motivation means/SDs for synthesis. The reported large effects are for writing outcomes, not motivation, and they are plausible relative to the provided pre/post means and SDs; they do not resemble an implausible d≈19. Therefore this study should be excluded from any quantitative synthesis specifically targeting ChatGPT-based writing feedback in high school, and also excluded from any motivation meta-analysis because it lacks usable quantitative motivation outcome data.
quality_tier_rationale: The paper reports a control-group pre/post design with baseline equivalence and claims stratified random assignment, which would ordinarily suggest an RCT. But credibility is weakened by internal inconsistencies (quasi-experimental vs randomized), limited methodological transparency, no confidence intervals or raw data, unclear peer-review rigor, and several features that warrant caution about authenticity and reproducibility; therefore it should not be treated as a clean high-quality RCT.
impact_tier_rationale: If taken at face value, the reported writing effects are large (Cohen's d=1.40-1.75; between-group η²=0.44-0.48), indicating substantial positive impact on academic writing outcomes in this university EFL sample. However, the impact rating reflects reported magnitude only and should be interpreted cautiously given the study's credibility concerns.

interventions.use_case: Grammarly premium used as an AI-powered L2 writing assistant for university EFL students to draft and revise argumentative essays over 12 weeks, with automated feedback on grammar, style, clarity, coherence, and readability.
Automated written feedback on student essays, paired with usage analytics such as revision frequency and time-on-task to study links between feedback uptake and writing gains.

finding.finding_summary: This paper reports large pre-post improvements for the Grammarly group on L2 writing outcomes in a university sample (n=30 experimental; n=30 control), including grammar accuracy (5.12±0.86 to 7.08±0.78, t=9.57, d=1.75), coherence (5.30±0.73 to 6.92±0.81, t=8.11, d=1.48), and syntactic complexity (4.98±0.92 to 6.73±0.84, t=7.66, d=1.40). Between-group gain-score comparisons also favored Grammarly: grammar gain 1.96±0.67 vs 0.84±0.61 (t=7.12, p<0.001, η²=0.47), coherence gain 1.62±0.63 vs 0.68±0.55 (t=6.81, p<0.001, η²=0.44), and syntactic complexity gain 1.75±0.61 vs 0.82±0.58 (t=7.36, p<0.001, η²=0.48). However, the reporting contains important credibility concerns: despite calling the design quasi-experimental, the paper also claims stratified random assignment; no CONSORT-style details, allocation concealment, preregistration, raw data, or confidence intervals are provided, and the claimed effects are large but not implausibly extreme like d≈19.
finding.measure: IELTS-style rubric scores for grammar accuracy, coherence, and syntactic complexity; Coh-Metrix indices including mean sentence length, referential cohesion, and lexical diversity (MTLD).
finding.study_size: n=60 total; experimental n=30, control n=30
finding.effect_size: Within-group Cohen's d=1.40-1.75 for experimental group; between-group η²=0.44-0.48 on gain scores
finding.std_deviation: Reported for key outcomes: e.g., grammar accuracy pre SD=0.86, post SD=0.78; coherence pre SD=0.73, post SD=0.81; syntactic complexity pre SD=0.92, post SD=0.84

finding.finding_summary: The study qualitatively reports higher motivation, confidence, and trust in AI feedback among 15 interviewed Grammarly users, with participants describing greater willingness to revise and reduced dependence on delayed teacher feedback. These findings are narrative only: no motivation scale, no pre/post quantitative statistics, and no effect sizes are provided, so the evidence for motivation is suggestive rather than estimable for meta-analysis.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes on motivation, self-efficacy, trust in AI feedback, and perceived engagement.
finding.study_size: n=15 interviewed from the experimental group; n=60 overall in the study

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests improved self-regulated revision behavior through frequent iterative editing with Grammarly, and regression models indicate revision frequency (β=0.59, p<0.001) and time-on-task (β=0.38, p=0.004) jointly explained 54% of variance in writing improvement (combined model R²=0.54, F(2,27)=15.89, p<0.001). However, these are process indicators within the experimental group rather than a validated between-group measure of self-regulation or metacognition.
finding.measure: Behavioral analytics: revision frequency, time-on-task, and qualitative comments about independent revision/self-monitoring.
finding.std_deviation: Revisions per essay mean=18.3 SD=4.2; time spent per essay mean=42.7 min SD=8.3
